meta.title: How to Pay Car Insurance in Texas & New Mexico — Safe House Insurance
meta.desc: How car insurance payments work — paying in full vs monthly, what happens if you miss a payment, and how to avoid a lapse. Written for Texas and New Mexico drivers.

hero.h1: Paying for car insurance, without losing your coverage
hero.lede:
How the payment actually works, what a lapse really costs in Texas and
        New Mexico, and what to do in the week you cannot pay. Written by licensed agents
        who spend most of their day on exactly this.

key.l1:
Nearly every carrier takes a card, a bank transfer or a check. Cash is usually
            an office-only option and never something to mail.
key.l2:
Paying six months at once almost always costs less overall than paying monthly,
            because you skip the instalment fees.
key.l3:
Most carriers discount autopay. How much is different at every one, so ask
            yours rather than assuming.
key.l4:
A cancellation for non-payment is far more expensive than the payment. It follows
            you into your next policy’s price, and it can cost you the continuous-coverage
            discount you already had.
key.l5:
If you are going to be late, call before the due date. There is almost always
            something an agent can do beforehand and much less afterwards.

ways.p:
Payment methods are set by your insurance company, not by us — but across the
        carriers we place business with, these are the usual ones.

card.s:
The fastest, and what the online portals are built around. A card payment
            usually posts the same day.

ach.s:
Straight from a checking account. Most carriers reserve their best autopay
            discount for this rather than for cards.

check.s:
Accepted by most, but it has to arrive and clear before the due date, not
            be postmarked by it.

cash.s:
Some carriers take cash at an office or a payment centre. Never mail
            it — there is no way to prove it arrived.

full.p1:
Most policies here run six months. You can usually pay the whole term at once, or
        put money down and pay the rest in instalments. Paying in full costs less overall,
        because instalment plans add a fee to each payment and the down payment is often
        larger than one month’s share.
full.p2:
That does not make it the right answer for everybody, and an agent who tells you it
        always is has not asked about your month.

inFull.b: Paying in full makes sense when
inFull.l1: You have the whole amount without touching money you need for something else
inFull.l2: Your income is steady and predictable
inFull.l3: You would rather not think about it again for six months

monthly.l1: The full amount would leave you short somewhere that matters more
monthly.l2: Your income moves around week to week
monthly.l3: You would rather keep the cash available for an emergency
monthly.l4: You are between jobs or expecting a change soon

full.p3:
The mistake is not choosing monthly. It is choosing a
        monthly payment that is tight every single month — because the month it does not
        clear costs far more than the difference you saved.

miss.h2: What happens if you miss a payment
miss.p: Missing one is common and it is recoverable. What matters is how fast you move, and the timeline below is the shape of it at most carriers. The exact dates are on the notice your carrier sends you — they are set by that carrier and by state law, so read the notice rather than trusting a number you found online, including ours.

s1.p:
Coverage does not usually stop the moment a payment is missed. Most carriers
            allow a short window first, and you are still insured during it.

s2.p:
A letter, email or text with a date on it. That date is the one that matters —
            it is when coverage actually ends if nothing is paid.

s3.p:
From that date you are uninsured. Driving uninsured is illegal in both Texas and
            New Mexico, and a stop, an accident or a traffic camera in that gap is a much
            larger problem than the missed payment was.

s4.p:
Many carriers will put a recently cancelled policy back in force if you pay what
            is owed plus a fee, and some will not. It depends on the carrier and how long the
            gap has been. This is the point to call rather than to pay online and hope.

call.b: Call before you pay a cancelled policy.
call.p: A payment made after a cancellation date does not always reinstate the policy, and some carriers will hold the money against the balance while you keep driving with no coverage. One call tells you whether you need a reinstatement, a new policy, or just the payment. We do this every day — 915-503-1207.

lapse.h2: Why a lapse costs more than the payment
lapse.p1:
This is the part that surprises people. The money you did not pay is rarely the
        expensive bit — the gap in your record is.
lapse.p2:
Carriers price continuous coverage. Going without it, even briefly, moves you into a
        worse bracket at renewal and at every carrier you shop afterwards, and it can cost you
        a prior-insurance discount you already had. A lapse of a few days can follow your
        premium for years, which is why it is worth a phone call to avoid one.
lapse.p3:
On top of that, both states require you to carry liability while your vehicle is
        registered:

tx.span: Thousands: injury per person, injury per accident, property damage.

nm.span: The same three figures, at New Mexico’s limits.

lapse.p4:
Those are floors written into law, not recommendations —
        and a lapse means you were below them.

cant.h2: If you cannot pay this month
cant.p:
There is more room here than most people think, and almost all of it exists before
        the due date rather than after it.

s1.b: Call before the date, not after
s1.p:
Some carriers will move a due date or split a payment if you ask in advance.
            Very few will do anything once the policy has cancelled.

s2.b: Ask what a partial payment buys
s2.p:
Paying part of it sometimes pushes the cancellation date out far enough to reach
            your next payday. Ask what the minimum is to keep the policy alive.

s3.p:
If the premium is the problem rather than this month, that is a different fix. We
            can compare what several carriers would charge for the same coverage — and check
            whether you are missing a discount you qualify for.

s4.p:
Raising a deductible or dropping collision on an older car lowers the payment, and
            both have real consequences. Worth doing with an agent, not alone at midnight.

auto.p1:
Most carriers discount autopay, usually more for a bank account than for a card, and
        the amount is different at every one — ask yours what it is rather than assuming a
        figure. The bigger value is not the discount anyway. It is that a policy on autopay
        does not lapse because a text message went unread during a busy week.
auto.p2:
Two things worth doing at the same time: make sure the account behind it is one that
        will not be short on the due date, and keep the carrier’s texts turned on so a failed
        payment reaches you.

cta.p:
Enter your policy number and we will take you straight to your carrier’s payment
        page. Or call and we will walk you through it.
